notes.meaning: David challenges the judges and rulers who were supposed to defend what is right but failed to do their duty. He calls them sons of men to remind them that they are merely mortal and must answer to God for their choices. Their silence in the face of evil made them guilty before the Lord.

Instead of weighing out fair decisions in court, these leaders plan evil in secret and carry it out in public. Their wicked choices start in their hearts and show up as cruel acts against ordinary people. They turn the scales of justice into a tool for violence.

The psalmist shows how deeply corrupt the wicked have become, turning away from God right from the start. As soon as they are able to act and speak, their fallen nature shows in their lies. They quickly wander into sin instead of walking in God's ways.

differ.view: They understand this verse as a proof of original sin, teaching that every person is born alienated from God and bent toward evil.
Some read this not as a doctrinal statement about every newborn child, but as poetic exaggeration describing people who grow up to be unusually wicked.

notes.meaning: David compares the harmful words of corrupt leaders to deadly snake venom. They are like a stubborn cobra that deliberately refuses to listen to anything good. Their slander and false rulings poison the lives of innocent people.

A skilled snake charmer tries to tame a serpent with music, but these rulers refuse to be moved. They shut out sound advice, their own consciences, and the law of God. No reasoning or godly appeal can persuade them to leave their cruelty behind.

David asks God to disarm his violent enemies completely, using the picture of breaking the fangs of lions and snakes. When God knocks out their teeth, he strips away their ability to tear apart the innocent. The prayer leaves the judgment in God's hands rather than seeking personal revenge.

David prays that the power of the wicked will disappear quickly, like water soaking into desert sand. When they draw their bows to shoot at the innocent, he asks that their arrows snap or become blunt and harmless. God can easily cause all their dangerous schemes to fail.

The wicked are compared to a slug that wastes away in its slime as it crawls, and to a child born dead who never sees the light. These stark pictures ask God to bring an end to their harmful careers before they can hurt others. Their proud schemes will vanish without leaving anything lasting behind.

Travelers made cooking fires out of thorn branches, but a sudden desert windstorm could sweep the kindling away before the pot even grew warm. In the same way, God will suddenly blow away wicked oppressors in his anger. Their plans will be cut short before they ever taste the outcome.

God's people will rejoice when they see evil finally punished and truth defended. The picture of washing feet in blood is an ancient war image that means complete victory over cruel enemies. This joy does not come from spite, but from seeing the honor and justice of God upheld.

differ.view: Expressions that celebrate bloodshed belong to the older covenant and are completely foreign to the forgiving spirit Jesus calls Christians to live by.
Believers rightly rejoice in God's holy vengeance because it vindicates His justice, fulfills His promises, and delivers His church.

notes.meaning: When God steps in to defeat injustice, people everywhere will see that living for him is never useless. Observers will confess that there is a real God who governs and judges the earth. The faithful receive reassurance that their trust in God will be vindicated.
